terms.meaning: The shine of a metal, seen best on a freshly cut or polished surface.
Can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking.
Can be drawn into thin wires.
Makes a ringing sound when struck.
Breaks into pieces or powder when hit.
The slow damage of a metal surface by moist air, water or chemicals.
Coating iron with a thin layer of zinc so that it does not rust.

items.name: Shine of metals and non-metals
items.formula: Metals are generally lustrous. Most non-metals are dull.
items.example: Polished copper shines. A lump of coal does not.

items.name: Hitting with a hammer
items.formula: Metals flatten. Solid non-metals break into pieces.
items.example: Aluminium becomes foil. Sulfur turns to powder.

items.name: Drawing into wires
items.formula: Metals can be drawn into wires. Non-metals cannot.
items.example: Copper wires, and the strings of a sitar.

items.name: Sound when struck
items.formula: Metals ring. Non-metals give a dull thud.
items.example: School bells are made of metal.

items.name: Heat and electricity
items.formula: Metals are good conductors of both. Non-metals are generally poor conductors.
items.example: A pan is metal, and its handle is wood or plastic.

items.name: Metals that break the rules
items.formula: Sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife. Mercury is a liquid at room temperature.
items.example: Mercury has been used in thermometers.

items.name: How ductile is gold?
items.formula: 1 g of gold can be drawn into a wire about 2 km long.
items.example: So 3 g could make about 6 km of wire.

items.name: What iron needs to rust
items.formula: Both air and water.
items.example: A nail in moist air rusts. A nail in dry air does not, and neither does a nail under boiled water topped with oil.

items.name: Colour of corrosion
items.formula: Iron: brown. Copper: green. Silver: black.
items.example: An old copper vessel gets a green coat.

items.name: Preventing rust
items.formula: Keep air and water away: paint, oil, grease or galvanise.
items.example: A gate is painted so that it does not rust.

items.name: Iron Pillar of Delhi
items.formula: Built in the time of Chandragupta II, more than 1600 years ago, with hardly any rust.
items.example: It shows the metal-working skill of ancient India.

items.name: Oxides of metals
items.formula: Generally basic: they turn red litmus blue.
items.example: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame to give magnesium oxide, which is basic.

items.name: Oxides of non-metals
items.formula: Generally acidic: they turn blue litmus red.
items.example: Burning sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, which forms sulfurous acid in water.

items.name: Storing reactive elements
items.formula: Sodium is kept in kerosene. Phosphorus is kept in water.
items.example: Sodium reacts fiercely with air and water, and phosphorus catches fire in air.

items.name: Oxygen
items.formula: Needed for breathing and for burning.
items.example: All living beings depend on it.

items.name: Nitrogen
items.formula: Used to make fertilisers.
items.example: It helps plants to grow.

items.name: Chlorine
items.formula: Used to purify water.
items.example: It is added to clean drinking water.

items.name: Iodine
items.formula: A solution of it is an antiseptic for wounds.
items.example: It is put on a cut.

items.name: Zirconium and titanium
items.formula: Zirconium: atomic energy. Titanium: aerospace.
items.example: Both are special metals with modern uses.

items.name: Elements
items.formula: Metals and non-metals are elements: 118 are known, and none breaks down into simpler substances.
items.example: Plastic, glass and wood are not elements.

mistakes.text: Water alone does not rust iron, and neither does dry air. It takes both together.
Do not swap the oxides: metal oxide is basic, non-metal oxide is acidic.
Wood is neither malleable nor brittle, and it is not an element either.
Sodium goes in kerosene and phosphorus in water, not the other way round.
